hello.title: Hello, Crystal
hello.summary: Write your first Crystal programs: print text and numbers with puts, print and p, and let Crystal calculate.
hello.lesson.0: Crystal is a programming language that is easy to read and runs fast. A Crystal program is a list of instructions. The computer runs them from top to bottom, one line after the other. Your first instruction is `puts`: it prints a value and then starts a new line.
hello.lesson.2: Text in double quotes is called a **string**. Every `puts` prints its own line. In Crystal, strings always use double quotes, like `"Hi"`. Single quotes are only for one single character, like `'A'`.
hello.lesson.5: Numbers need no quotes. Crystal calculates with `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). Whole numbers are called **integers**. The result of `/` is always a number with a decimal point, a **float**: `7 / 2` is `3.5` and `6 / 2` is `3.0`. Use `//` to divide and drop the part after the decimal point: `7 // 2` is `3`. `%` gives the remainder of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.
hello.lesson.7: Quotes make a big difference. `"2"` with quotes is text, `2` without quotes is a number. `+` between two strings joins them, and `+` between two numbers adds them.
hello.lesson.9: Crystal checks your whole program before it runs it. This step is called **compiling**. `puts "Age: " + 30` does not compile, because `+` cannot join a string and a number. You see an error message, and no line of the program runs. You learn how to put numbers into text in the Strings unit.
hello.lesson.11: `print` prints a value **without** a new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `p` prints a value the way Crystal sees it: a string keeps its quotes. Programmers use `p` to check values while they work.
hello.lesson.13: Everything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Crystal ignores it. In this course, comments only show results, for example `puts 2 + 3 # 5`.
hello.card.0: `puts "Hi"` prints and starts a new line
hello.card.2: `p "Hi"` shows the value with its quotes: `"Hi"`
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints Hello and then starts a new line?
hello-1.explain: `puts` prints the value and starts a new line. `print` does not start a new line. Single quotes are only for one character, and `Hello` without quotes is not a string.
hello-3.explain: `//` divides and drops the part after the decimal point: 9 divided by 2 is 4.5, so the result is 4.
hello-4.explain: `/` always gives a float. 9 divided by 2 is `4.5`.
hello-5.explain: `/` always gives a float, so the program prints `3.0`. Use `6 // 2` to get `3`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.
hello-6.explain: `//` drops the part after the decimal point: `7 // 2` is `3`. `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and `7 % 2` is the remainder, `1`.
hello-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it does.
hello-7.pairs.0: prints and starts a new line
hello-7.pairs.2: shows the value as Crystal sees it
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 10 minus 4 and starts a new line.
hello-8.explain: `puts` prints the result, `6`, and starts a new line. Numbers need no quotes.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints: Hello, Crystal!
hello-9.explain: `print` keeps everything on one line. The last line uses `puts`, so the output ends with a new line.
hello-10.prompt: This program should print Start, 12 and End on three lines. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: Crystal multiplies with `*`, not with `x`. Write `puts 3 * 4`.
hello-11.explain: `p` shows the value the way Crystal sees it, so a string keeps its double quotes.
hello-12.prompt: This program should print: Hi, Sam! Which line has the bug?
hello-12.explain: Single quotes are only for one character, so `'Sam'` does not compile. Strings need double quotes: `print "Sam"`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, let Crystal find their types, and convert between Int32, Float64 and String.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. `=` stores the value on the right under the name on the left. After that, you can use the name instead of the value.
variables.lesson.2: You can give a variable a new value at any time. The new value can use the old one. `score += 5` is a short way to write `score = score + 5`. `-=` and `*=` work the same way.
variables.lesson.5: Crystal knows the **type** of every value before the program runs. You do not have to write the type: the compiler finds it from the value. This is called **type inference**. `typeof(x)` shows the type of `x`. Whole numbers are `Int32`, numbers with a decimal point are `Float64`, text is `String`, and `true` and `false` are `Bool`.
variables.lesson.7: The `32` in `Int32` means that the number uses 32 bits of memory. An `Int32` holds whole numbers up to about 2 billion. For bigger numbers, use `Int64`: write `_i64` after the number. You can put `_` between digits to make long numbers easier to read.
variables.lesson.9: You can also write the type yourself: `count : Int32 = 5`. Then `count` can only hold an `Int32`. If you later write `count = "eight"`, the program does not compile.
variables.lesson.11: Methods convert values to other types. `to_i` makes an integer, `to_f` makes a float, and `to_s` makes a string. `3.9.to_i` is `3`: it drops the part after the decimal point.
variables.lesson.13: A name that starts with an uppercase letter is a **constant**, for example `MAX = 100`. You cannot give a constant a new value. Names are case sensitive: `price` and `Price` are two different names.
variables-1.explain: First `x` is 4. Then `x` gets the value of `x * 3`, which is 12.
variables-2.explain: `2.5` has a decimal point, so its type is `Float64`.
variables-3.explain: `true` and `false` are the two values of the type `Bool`.
variables-4.explain: `count` can only hold an `Int32`. `"8"` is a `String` because of the quotes, so the program does not compile.
variables-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 43.
variables-5.explain: `to_i` turns the string into the integer 42, and 42 + 1 is 43. `to_f` gives `43.0`, and `to_s` keeps a string, which you cannot add to a number.
variables-6.explain: `to_i` drops the part after the decimal point. It does not round, so the result is 7.
variables-7.prompt: This program should print 12. Which line has the bug?
variables-7.explain: Names are case sensitive. `Price` with an uppercase P is not the variable `price`. Write `puts price * amount`.
variables-8.prompt: Match each type with its values.
variables-9.prompt: Build a line that creates the variable limit with the fixed type Int32 and the value 10.
variables-9.explain: The type comes after the name and a colon: `limit : Int32 = 10`.
variables-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 20.
variables-10.explain: 5 plus 5 is 10, and 10 times 2 is 20. In the other order you get 5 times 2 plus 5, which is 15.
variables-11.explain: A name that starts with an uppercase letter is a constant. `max` is a normal variable, and `==` compares values.
variables-12.prompt: This program should print 3.5. Which line has the bug?
variables-12.explain: `a.to_s` is still the string `"7"`, and you cannot divide a string. Write `b = a.to_i`, then `7 / 2` is `3.5`.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Put values into text with #{}, and work with strings: size, upcase, includes? and single characters.
strings.lesson.0: **Interpolation** puts values into a string. Inside double quotes, write `#{` and `}` around a variable or a calculation. Crystal replaces it with the value, also when the value is a number. Here `#` does not start a comment.
strings.lesson.2: Strings have **methods**. You call a method with a dot after the value. `size` gives the number of characters. `upcase` and `downcase` change letters to uppercase or lowercase, `capitalize` makes only the first letter uppercase, and `reverse` turns the string around.
strings.lesson.4: A method whose name ends with `?` answers a question with `true` or `false`. `includes?` checks if a text contains another text. `starts_with?` and `ends_with?` check the start and the end. `empty?` checks if a string has no characters.
strings.lesson.7: `[]` with a number, the **index**, gets one character. Counting starts at `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `-1` is the last one. A single character has the type `Char` and is written in single quotes, like `'C'`.
strings.lesson.9: `+` joins two strings, and `*` repeats a string. `strip` removes spaces at the start and at the end. You can call several methods one after the other: Crystal runs them from left to right.
strings.lesson.11: Uppercase and lowercase letters are different characters. `"Crystal".includes?("crystal")` is `false`. Call `downcase` first if case should not matter.
strings.card.0: `"Hi #{name}"` puts a value into a string
strings.card.3: `s[0]` is the first character, a `Char` like `'C'`
strings-1.explain: `#{name}` is replaced by the value of `name`.
strings-2.explain: `size` counts the characters: h, e, l, l, o.
strings-3.explain: Uppercase `C` and lowercase `c` are different characters, so the text does not contain `crystal`.
strings-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints: Total: 6
strings-4.explain: Only `#{` and `}` start interpolation. The other options are printed as they are.
strings-5.explain: Counting starts at 0. `[0]` is `C`, so `[1]` is the second character, `r`.
strings-6.explain: `*` repeats a string. The copies are joined without spaces.
strings-7.prompt: This program should print: Hello, Kim! Which line has the bug?
strings-7.explain: Names are case sensitive. The variable is `name`, not `Name`. Write `"Hello, #{name}!"`.
strings-8.prompt: Match each method with what it does.
strings-9.prompt: The variable word holds "crystal". Build a line that prints: CRYSTAL!
strings-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints: Hi, ADA
strings-10.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before, so it must come after it.
strings-11.explain: `strip` removes the spaces at both ends, so `"ok"` is left. It has 2 characters.
strings-12.prompt: This program should print the first character, C. Which line has the bug?
strings-12.explain: Counting starts at 0, so the first character is `word[0]`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program decide with if, elsif, else, unless, case and the ternary operator, and handle nil safely.
conditions.lesson.0: A comparison gives a `Bool`. `==` checks if two values are equal, `!=` checks if they are different. `<` means less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal, `>=` greater than or equal. Be careful: `=` stores a value, `==` compares.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The lines between `if` and `end` are the **body**; indent them by two spaces. The body after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.
conditions.lesson.4: `elsif` checks another condition. Crystal checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first body whose condition is `true`.
conditions.lesson.6: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is true. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and back. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: its body runs when the condition is `false`. For one line, you can write `if` or `unless` at the end of the line.
conditions.lesson.8: `case` compares one value with several `when` branches. A `when` can list several values, separated by commas, or a **range** like `1..5`, which means all numbers from 1 to 5. `else` runs when no `when` matches.
conditions.lesson.10: The **ternary operator** is a short `if` with `else` in one line: `condition ? a : b`. It gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`.
conditions.lesson.12: Sometimes there is no value. Crystal uses `nil` for this. `"crystal".index('s')` gives the position of the first `s`, or `nil` if there is none. `if pos` runs its body only when `pos` is not `nil`, and inside the body Crystal knows that `pos` is a number. `nil?` checks if a value is `nil`. The compiler does not let you calculate with a value that might be `nil`, so you cannot forget this check.
conditions.card.2: `&&` and, `||` or, `!` not, `unless` means if not
conditions-1.explain: 8 is not greater than 10, but it is greater than 5, so the `elsif` body runs.
conditions-2.prompt: Which operator checks if two values are equal?
conditions-2.explain: `==` compares two values. `=` stores a value in a variable, and `!=` checks if values are different.
conditions-3.explain: `&&` needs both sides to be true. `3 > 2` is true, but `2 > 5` is false, so the result is `false`.
conditions-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Closed.
conditions-4.explain: `day < 6` is false for 7, so with `if` the `else` body runs. `unless` would print `Open`, and `elsif` cannot start a decision.
conditions-5.explain: 4 % 2 is 0, so the condition is true and the ternary operator gives the first value.
conditions-6.explain: 3 is in the range `3..4`, so the second `when` matches.
conditions-7.prompt: This program should print Adult. Which line has the bug?
conditions-7.explain: Greater than or equal is written `>=`. Write `if age >= 18`.
conditions-8.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
conditions-8.pairs.1: at least one side is true
conditions-8.pairs.2: turns true into false and back
conditions-8.pairs.3: runs code when the condition is false
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Cold.
conditions-9.explain: First store the value. 5 is not greater than 15, so the body after `else` runs.
conditions-10.prompt: Build a line that prints Hot only when temp is greater than 30.
conditions-10.explain: `if` at the end of a line runs the line only when the condition is true.
conditions-11.explain: There is no `z` in `"hello"`, so `index` gives `nil`, and `nil?` is `true`.
conditions-12.prompt: This program should print: Found at 1. Which line has the bug?
conditions-12.explain: `+` cannot join a string and a number. Use interpolation: `puts "Found at #{pos}"`.
loops.title: Loops and ranges
loops.summary: Repeat code with times, each and while, count with ranges, and control loops with break and next.
loops.lesson.0: Programs often repeat things. `3.times` runs code three times. The code between `do` and `end` is a **block**: a piece of code that you give to a method.
loops.lesson.2: A block can take a **parameter**, a name between two `|` bars. `times` passes the number of the round to the block. It starts counting at `0`.
loops.lesson.5: A **range** is a sequence of numbers. `1..3` contains 1, 2 and 3. With three dots, `1...3` stops before the end and contains only 1 and 2. `each` runs the block once for every number. For a short block, you can write `{` and `}` instead of `do` and `end`.
loops.lesson.7: Ranges have useful methods. `sum` adds up all numbers, and `includes?` checks if a number is in the range.
loops.lesson.10: `while` repeats its body as long as the condition is `true`. Change a variable in the body so that the condition becomes `false` at some point. Otherwise the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.12: `break` leaves a loop at once. `next` skips the rest of the body and goes on with the next round. `odd?` and `even?` check if a number is odd or even.
loops.card.3: `while x < 10` … `end` repeats while the condition is true
loops.card.4: `break` leaves the loop, `next` skips to the next round
loops-1.explain: `i` takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. Their sum is 6.
loops-2.prompt: How many lines does this print?
loops-2.explain: `1...5` stops before 5, so it contains 1, 2, 3 and 4.
loops-4.statement: This program prints 1, 2 and 3 on three lines.
loops-4.explain: The loop runs while `n` is at most 3. After printing 3, `n` becomes 4 and the loop stops.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the numbers from 1 to 5.
loops-5.explain: Two dots include the end, so `1..5` contains 5. `1...5` stops at 4.
loops-6.prompt: This program should print 3, 2 and 1 on three lines. Which line has the bug?
loops-6.explain: With `>=`, the loop also runs for 0 and prints it. Write `while n > 0`.
loops-7.explain: `print` adds no new line. When `n` is 4, `break` leaves the loop, so only 1, 2 and 3 are printed.
loops-8.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 2, 4 and 6 on three lines.
loops-9.explain: `next` must come before `puts`, so odd numbers are skipped before they are printed.
loops-10.prompt: Build a line that prints Hi five times.
loops-10.explain: `5.times` runs the block in `{` and `}` five times.
loops-11.explain: There are 5 even numbers from 1 to 10: 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
loops-12.prompt: This program should print Round 1, Round 2 and Round 3. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: `times` starts counting at 0, so the program prints Round 0 to Round 2. Write `puts "Round #{i + 1}"`.
methods.title: Methods
methods.summary: Write your own methods with def, restrict argument types, return values, and use default and named arguments.
methods.lesson.0: A **method** is a piece of code with a name. You define it once with `def` and the name, and end it with `end`. After that, you run it by writing its name. This is called **calling** the method.
methods.lesson.2: A method can take **parameters** in parentheses. `name : String` is a **type restriction**: the method only accepts a `String` for `name`. When you call the method, the values in parentheses are the **arguments**.
methods.lesson.4: A method gives back a **return value**: the value of its last line. You can write the type of the return value after the parentheses, like `: Int32`. Then the compiler checks that the method really returns an `Int32`.
methods.lesson.6: `return` leaves the method at once and gives back the value after it. This is useful to handle a special case first.
methods.lesson.9: A parameter can have a **default value**: `name = "World"`. When you call the method without this argument, the default value is used. You can also write the parameter names in a call, like `area(height: 2, width: 5)`. With **named arguments**, the order does not matter.
methods.lesson.11: In Crystal, a method whose name ends with `?` returns `true` or `false`, like `even?`. You can write such methods yourself.
methods.lesson.13: Type restrictions protect you. `square("4")` does not compile, because `"4"` is a `String` and `square` needs an `Int32`. The compiler finds this mistake before the program runs.
methods.card.0: `def name(x : Int32) : Int32` … `end` defines a method
methods.card.1: The last line is the return value; `return` leaves early
methods-1.explain: The last line of the method, `n * 2`, is its return value: 7 times 2 is 14.
methods-2.explain: The call has no argument, so `name` gets its default value, `"you"`.
methods-3.explain: `square` only accepts an `Int32`, but `"3"` is a `String`, so the compiler stops with an error.
methods-4.prompt: Complete the method so the program prints 5.
methods-4.explain: The last line is the return value, so it must be the sum `a + b`. `puts` returns `nil` and a string is not an `Int32`, so the other options do not compile.
methods-5.explain: 25 is not less than 10, so `return` does not run, and the method returns the last line, `"big"`.
methods-6.prompt: This program should print 9. Which line has the bug?
methods-6.explain: `n * n` is an `Int32`, not a `String`, so the program does not compile. Write `def square(n : Int32) : Int32`.
methods-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
methods-7.pairs.1: leaves the method with a value
methods-7.pairs.2: the type of the return value
methods-7.pairs.3: a parameter with a default value
methods-8.prompt: Put the lines in order: define the method first, then call it, so the program prints 12.
methods-8.explain: The variable `sum` must exist before you use it. The last line of the method, `sum * 2`, is the return value: (2 + 4) times 2 is 12.
methods-9.prompt: Build the first line of the method half: it takes an Int32 called n and returns a Float64.
methods-9.explain: First the name and the parameter with its type, then the return type after the parentheses.
methods-10.prompt: The method is `def area(width : Int32, height : Int32)`. Which call works?
methods-10.explain: The call needs two `Int32` arguments. Named arguments must use the parameter names, `width` and `height`.
methods-11.explain: 17 is not greater than or equal to 18, so the method returns `false`.
methods-12.prompt: This program should print: Hello, World! Which line has the bug?
methods-12.explain: The default value is text, so it needs quotes. Write `def greet(name = "World")`.
collections.title: Arrays and hashes
collections.summary: Keep many values in arrays and hashes, and work with them using each, map, select and sum.
collections.lesson.0: An **array** is an ordered list of values. Write the values between `[` and `]`, separated by commas. `[]` with an index gets one item: counting starts at `0`, and `-1` is the last item. `size` gives the number of items.
collections.lesson.2: `<<` adds an item at the end. All items of an array have the same type: `[1, 2, 3]` is an `Array(Int32)`. An empty array has no items to show its type, so you write it yourself: `[] of String`.
collections.lesson.4: `each` runs a block once for every item. The block parameter holds the current item.
collections.lesson.6: `map` makes a new array with the result of the block for every item. `select` keeps only the items for which the block is `true`. `sum` adds up all items, and `includes?` checks if an item is in the array. `&.even?` is a short way to write the block `{ |n| n.even? }`.
collections.lesson.8: `nums[10]` stops the program with an error when the array has no item at index 10. Add a `?` to get `nil` instead: `nums[10]?`.
collections.lesson.10: A **hash** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. Write them between `{` and `}` with `=>` between key and value. `ages["Ada"]` reads the value for the key `"Ada"`, and `ages["Cy"] = 41` adds or changes a pair. `ages["Dan"]?` gives `nil` when the key is missing, and `has_key?` checks if a key exists.
collections.lesson.12: `each` on a hash passes two values to the block: the key and the value.
collections.card.1: `[] of String` is an empty array of strings
collections-1.explain: Counting starts at 0, so `nums[1]` is the second item, 8.
collections-2.explain: `map` makes a new array with the square of every item.
collections-3.explain: `select(&.odd?)` keeps 5 and 9, and their sum is 14.
collections-4.explain: The key `"Bob"` is missing. With `?`, the hash gives `nil` instead of stopping with an error.
collections-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.
collections-5.explain: `<<` adds `"c"` at the end, so the array has 3 items. `+` cannot add a string to an array, and `=` replaces the array with the string `"c"`.
collections-6.prompt: This program should print 6. Which line has the bug?
collections-6.explain: An empty array needs its type. Write `nums = [] of Int32`.
collections-7.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
collections-7.pairs.3: the value for the key, or nil
collections-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints apple: 3 and pear: 1 on two lines.
collections-8.explain: First create the hash, then loop over it. The block gets the key and the value of every pair.
collections-9.prompt: The variable nums holds [1, 2, 3]. Build a line that prints [2, 4, 6].
collections-9.explain: `map` runs the block for every item and collects the results in a new array.
collections-10.prompt: Which line creates an empty array for strings?
collections-10.explain: An empty array needs its type, written with `of`. `{}` is for hashes, and `[String]` is an array that contains the type `String` itself.
collections-11.explain: The second line changes the value for `"Ada"` to 37, and 37 + 25 is 62.
collections-12.prompt: This program should print red, green and blue on three lines. Which line has the bug?
collections-12.explain: The block parameter is called `c`, there is no variable `color`. Write `puts c`.
classes.title: Classes and structs
classes.summary: Build your own types with class and struct, store data in instance variables, and use getter and property.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** is a plan for **objects**. An object keeps data together with the methods that work on it. Class names start with an uppercase letter. `Dog.new("Rex")` creates a new object, and Crystal calls the method `initialize` with the arguments.
classes.lesson.2: `@name` is an **instance variable**. Every object has its own copy, and all methods of the object can use it. The short form `def initialize(@name : String)` stores the argument in `@name` directly.
classes.lesson.5: Code outside the class cannot read instance variables. `getter name : String` creates a method `name` that reads `@name`. `property score : Int32` creates a method to read `@score` and one to change it.
classes.lesson.7: A `getter` can only read. `player.name = "Bob"` does not compile, because there is no method to change `name`. Use `property` when code outside the class should change a value.
classes.lesson.8: Methods can change instance variables. `getter count = 0` creates `@count` with the start value `0` and a method to read it.
classes.lesson.11: A **struct** looks like a class, but it is **copied** when you store it in another variable. Objects of a class are **shared**: two variables can point to the same object. In this program, changing `b` does not change the struct `a`, but changing `y` also changes the object `x`.
classes.lesson.13: Use a struct for small values like a point or a color. Use a class for things that change over time, like a player or a shopping cart.
classes.card.2: `getter name : String` reads, `property score : Int32` reads and writes
classes.card.3: `@name` is an instance variable, one per object
classes.card.4: `struct` values are copied, `class` objects are shared
classes-1.explain: `initialize` stores `"Tom"` in `@name`, and `hello` returns the string with the name in it.
classes-2.prompt: Which method runs when you write `Dog.new("Rex")`?
classes-2.explain: `new` creates the object and then calls `initialize` with the arguments.
classes-3.explain: `getter` only creates a method to read `title`. To change it, the class needs `property title : String`.
classes-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 8.
classes-4.explain: `bag.size = 8` changes the value, so the class needs `property`. With `getter` you can only read it.
classes-5.explain: `@count` starts at 0. The two calls add 2 and 5, so it is 7.
classes-6.explain: `Point` is a struct, so `b = a` makes a copy. Changing `b` does not change `a`.
classes-7.prompt: This program should print Rex. Which line has the bug?
classes-7.explain: Without `@`, the argument is not stored, so `@name` never gets a value and the program does not compile. Write `def initialize(@name : String)`.
classes-8.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
classes-8.pairs.2: creates a method to read a value
